parole.significato: Used to form female equivalents.
parole.testo: From Middle English -esse, borrowed from Old French -esse, from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa). Displaced Old English -en (feminine suffix of nouns).

parole.significato: Used to form diminutives, loosely construed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -et, from Old French -et, from Late Latin -ittus, -ettus.

parole.significato: The office or dominion of an abbot or abbess.
parole.testo: From A.D. 1250 in Middle English abbey, abbeye (“convent headed by an abbot”) (compare archaic English abbaye), itself borrowed from Old French abaïe, abbaïe, abeïe, abbeïe (Modern French abbaye) from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, from Classical Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbacy

parole.significato: The act of washing something.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablucioun (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French ablution, and its source, Late Latin ablūtiō (“a washing away”), from abluō (“wash away”), from ab- (“away”) + lavō (“wash”).

parole.significato: To deprive; to cut off.
parole.testo: From Middle English abreggen, abregge, abrigge (“curtail, lessen”), from Old French abregier, abreger, from Late Latin abbreviō, abbreviāre (“make brief”). Doublet of abbreviate.

parole.significato: To keep (oneself) away.
parole.testo: From Middle English absenten, from Old French absenter, from Late Latin absentāre (“keep away, be away”).

parole.significato: Hell; the infernal pit; the great deep; the primal chaos.
parole.testo: From Middle English abime, from Old French abisme from Late Latin *abyssimus, a superlative of abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos). Cognate to French abîme. See also abyss.

parole.significato: One who has received the highest of the four minor orders in the Catholic Church, being ordained to carry the wine, wat…
parole.testo: From Middle English acolite, acolit, from Old French acolyt and Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).

parole.significato: To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English a(d)monisshen (adapted through -ishen (“-ish”) from earlier amonesten), from Old French amonester (modern French admonester), from an unattested Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, from Latin admoneō (“to remind, warn”), from ad- + moneō (“to warn, advise”).

parole.significato: adultery
parole.testo: From Middle English avoutrie, from Old French avouterie, variant (perhaps influenced by vout, vut (“vow”)) of aouterie, aolterie, from Late Latin adulterium. Doublet of adultery, which replaced it in modern English.

parole.significato: Friendly; kind; sweet; gracious.
parole.testo: From Middle English amyable, from Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”, verb). parole.significato: To disturb or irritate, especially by continued or repeated acts; to bother with unpleasant deeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English anoyen, from Old French anoier (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin inodiāre (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin odium (“loathing, hatred”). Displaced native Old English dreċċan, gremman.

parole.significato: Unconsciousness or incapacity resulting from a cerebral hemorrhage or stroke.
parole.testo: Late Middle English from Old French apoplexie, from Late Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía, “madness; apoplexy, paralysis”), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”) + -ία (-ía, nominal suffix). See plague.

parole.significato: An abscess; a pustulent swelling.
parole.testo: From Middle English aposteme (“a swelling, inflamation”), from Old French aposteme and Late Latin apostēma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστημα (apóstēma, “abcesse”) (source of Modern Greek απόστημα (apóstima, “abscess”)), related to ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to remove”).

parole.significato: A missionary, or leader of a religious mission, especially one in the early Christian Church (but see Apostle).
parole.testo: From Middle English apostle, from Old French apostle, from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”). Merged with Old English apostol, borrowing from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: To perceive.
parole.testo: From Middle English aperceiven, from Old French aperceveir, apercevoir, from Late Latin *appercipiō, from ad- + percipiō.

parole.significato: To belong to or be a part of, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom; to relate to.
parole.testo: From Middle English apperteinen, apertenen, borrowed from Old French apartenir (French appartenir), from Late Latin appertinēre, from ad (“to”) + Latin pertinēre (“to reach to, belong”). More at pertain.

parole.significato: To determine the value or worth of (something), particularly as a person appointed for this purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English apreisen, from Old French aprisier (“apraise, set a price on”) (compare modern French apprécier), from Late Latin appretiare, from ad- + Latin pretium (“price, value”) (English precious), from which also appreciate, a doublet.

parole.significato: A trainee, especially in a skilled trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English apprentice, apprentesse, apprentyse, apprentis, from Old French aprentis, plural of aprentif, from Old French aprendre (verb), Late Latin apprendō, from Classical Latin apprehendō. parole.significato: To come or go near, in place or time; to move toward; to advance nearer; to draw nigh.

parole.significato: A steel crossbow.
parole.testo: From Middle English arblast, from Old French arbaleste (modern arbalète), from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus + ballista.

parole.significato: A wooden crossbow with a special drawing mechanism, used to fire bolts, stones, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arblast, from late Old English arblast, from Old French arbaleste (modern French arbalète), from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”).

parole.significato: To attack with harsh words or violent force.
parole.testo: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assault.

parole.significato: Someone who attacks or assails another violently, or criminally.
parole.testo: From Old French assaillant, from the verb assaillir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“to, towards”) + salīre (“to jump”). Equivalent to assail + -ant.

parole.significato: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English assaut, from Old French noun assaut, derived from the past participle of the verb assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assail. Spelling Latinized around 1530 to add an l.

parole.significato: Begone; depart; used in contempt or abhorrence.
parole.testo: First used 1275–1325; Middle English, from Old French avant (“to the front”).

parole.significato: adultery
parole.testo: From Middle English avoutrie, from Old French avouterie, variant (perhaps influenced by vout, vut (“vow”)) of aouterie, aolterie, from Late Latin adulterium. Doublet of adultery, which replaced it in modern English.

parole.significato: To perform the sacrament of baptism by sprinkling or pouring water over someone or immersing them in water.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptisen, baptizen, from Old French baptiser, batisier, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptizāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptize”).

parole.significato: To hit with a bat or (figuratively) as if with a bat.
parole.testo: From Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), from Old French batre (“to beat”), from Late Latin battere, from Latin battuere, of uncertain origin; perhaps of Germanic or Celtic origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2. Compare batter, battery.

parole.significato: A tower or steeple typically containing bells, especially as part of a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English belfry, bellfray, belfray, berfrey, barfray, from Old French belfroi, berfroi, berfrey, from Late Latin berfrēdus, from Frankish *bergafriþu, from Proto-Germanic *bergafriþuz, equivalent to barrow + frith. parole.significato: Beast-like.
parole.testo: From Middle English bestial, from Old French bestial, from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”) (whence English beast).

parole.significato: Censure.
parole.testo: From Middle English blame, borrowed from Old French blame, blasme, produced from the verb blasmer, which in turn is derived from Late Latin blastēmāre, variant of blasphēmāre, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). parole.significato: To commit blasphemy; to speak against God or religious doctrine.
parole.testo: From Middle English blasfemen, blasphemen, from Old French blasfemer, from Late Latin blasphēmāre, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Doublet of blame.

parole.significato: Cotton wool made from raw cotton, typically used as padding in clothing or as a stopper.
parole.testo: From Old French bombace (“cotton, cotton wadding”), from Late Latin bombax (“cotton”), a variant of bombyx (“silkworm”), from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silkworm”), possibly related to Middle Persian pmbk' (“cotton”), from a Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: Cotton, or cotton wool.
parole.testo: From Old French bombace (“cotton, cotton wadding”), from Late Latin bombax (“cotton”), a variant of bombyx (“silkworm”), from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silkworm”), possibly related to Middle Persian pmbk' (“cotton”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to twist, wind”.

parole.significato: A container, typically made of glass or plastic and having a tapered neck, used primarily for holding liquids.
parole.testo: From Middle English botel (“bottle, flask, wineskin”), from Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula, diminutive of buttis (“cask”). Doublet of botija. Displaced native pinne and non-native Old English ampella. Partially displaced Old English flasce.

parole.significato: The woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing.
parole.testo: From Middle English branche, braunche, bronche, from Old French branche, branke, from Late Latin branca (“footprint”, later also “paw, claw”) (whence Middle High German pranke, German Pranke (“paw”)), of unknown origin. parole.significato: A partition in a coal mine, made from wood or from canvas sheeting coated in tar.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bretage, bretace, from Old French bretesce, bretesche, breteske, from Late Latin brittisca.

parole.significato: A purse.

parole.significato: A coarse woolen cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English burel, burrel, borel, from Old French burel, diminutive of *bure (compare Middle French bure (“coarse woolen cloth”), French bourre (“hair, fluff”)), from Late Latin burra (“wool, fluff, shaggy cloth, coarse fabric”). parole.significato: The uppermost part of a column.

parole.significato: A chief or leader.
parole.testo: From Middle English capitain, capteyn, from Old French capitaine, from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput (“head”) (English cap). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of chieftain, also from Old French.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Cynara cardunculus of prickly perennial plants which has leaf stalks eaten as a vegetable, re…
parole.testo: From Middle English cardoun, from Old French cardon, from Late Latin cardōnem, from Latin cardus, alternative form of carduus (“thistle”). Respelled on analogy of -oon nouns. Doublet of cardon and chard.

parole.significato: Relating to the physical and especially sexual appetites or activities.
parole.testo: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).

parole.significato: Any of various freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English carpe (“the common carp (Cyprinus carpio)”), from Old French carpe, from Late Latin carpa, possibly from Proto-West Germanic *karpo (possibly due to the introduction from the fish from the Danube into England in the 14th century; whence Middle Low German karpe and Old High G

parole.significato: To render moot or void; to annul; to reject
parole.testo: From Middle English cassen, from Old French casser, from Late Latin cassō, from Latin cassus (“empty, hollow”), and perhaps influenced by quassō (“to shake, shatter”).

parole.significato: A systematic list of books, names, pictures, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English cathaloge, from Old French catalogue, from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “enrollment, register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, make a list”), from κατα- (kata-, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to say, to speak, to tell”). parole.significato: Open countryside, or an area of open countryside.
parole.testo: From Old French champaigne, from Late Latin campānia.

parole.significato: The rank or post of a chancellor.
parole.testo: From Middle English chancelrie, from Old French chancelerie (Modern French chancellerie), from Late Latin cancellaria. Doublet of chancery.

parole.significato: A place of worship, smaller than or subordinate to a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English chapele, chapel, from Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Doublet of capelle. parole.significato: The amount of money levied for a service.
parole.testo: From Middle English chargen, from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”); see car. Doublet of cargo.

parole.significato: The outermost liturgical vestment worn by clergy for celebrating Eucharist or Mass, equivalent to the phelonion of the…
parole.testo: From Middle English chesible, from Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).

parole.significato: The entrails of an animal, especially when used as a food ingredient; offal.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English chaudon, chaudoun, chaudron (“sauce made from chopped entrails”), from Old French chaudun (“animal entrails; sauce made from such entrails”) (modern French chaudin (“wrapping of sausages made from pigs’ intestines; Louisiana meat dish cooked in a pig’s stomach”)), from Late

parole.significato: To violate rules in order to gain, or attempt to gain, advantage from a situation.
parole.testo: Verb from Middle English achetan, variant of escheten, from Old French escheat, past participle of escheoir, escheoiter, from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Displaced native Old English beswīcan. Noun from verb and/or Middle English chete, aphetic f

parole.significato: A leader of a clan or tribe.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheveteyn, cheftayne, from Old French chevetaine, from Late Latin capitaneus (English captain), from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of captain; related to chief.

parole.testo: From Middle English chymeneye, chymneye, chymene, from Old French cheminee, from Late Latin camīnāta, from Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos, “furnace”). Doublet of chimenea.

parole.significato: A kind of belt or other girdle.
parole.testo: From Middle English sengle, from Old French sengle, cengle (Modern French sangle), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum (“girdle”), from cingere (“to gird”). Doublet of cinch. Compare also Middle English kyngle, kyngll (“girdle, brooch”) from Old Norse kinga (“brooch”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a circle.
parole.testo: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier (French circulaire), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”). By surface analysis, circle + -ar.

parole.significato: A body of persons, such as priests, who are trained and ordained for religious service.
parole.testo: From Middle English clergie (attested in the 13th century), from Old French clergie (“learned men”), from Late Latin clēricātus, from Latin clēricus (“one ordained for religious services”), from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, “of the clergy”). Equivalent to cleric + -ate.

parole.significato: An event or occurrence that signifies an ending.
parole.testo: From Middle English closure, from Old French closure, from Late Latin clausura, from Latin claudere (“to close”); see clausure and cloture (etymological doublets) and close.

parole.significato: An assistant or helper.

parole.testo: From Middle English cohabitacioun, from Old French cohabitacion and Late Latin cohabitātiō. By surface analysis, co- + habitation.

parole.significato: Clothes that encircle the neck.
parole.testo: From Middle English coler, borrowed from Old French coler (Modern French collier), from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris, from collum (“neck”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐍃 (hals, “neck”), Old English heals (“neck”). Compare Spanish cuello (“neck”). More at halse. Doublet of collet.

parole.significato: The act of combining, the state of being combined or the result of combining.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English combinacioun, combynacyoun, from Old French combination, from Late Latin combīnātiō. Morphologically combine + -ation.

parole.significato: Contentment, ease.
parole.testo: From Middle English comfort, from Old French cunfort, confort, from the stem of Late Latin confortō. It replaced Old English frofor, Middle English frovre.

parole.significato: To relieve the distress or suffering of; to provide comfort to.
parole.testo: From Middle English comforten, from Old French conforter, from Late Latin confortō (“to strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: A spoken or written remark.
parole.testo: From Middle English coment, comment, from Old French coment (“commentary”), from Late Latin commentum (“comment, interpretation”), from Classical Latin commentum (“invention, fabrication”).

parole.significato: A team; a group of people who work together for a common purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English companye (“a team; companionship”), from Old French compaignie (“companionship”) (Modern French: compagnie), possibly from Late Latin *compania, but this word is not attested. parole.significato: One who drinks (alcoholic beverages) with another; a fellow drinker.
parole.testo: From Old French compotateur, from Late Latin compōtātōr, compōtātōrem, from Latin com-, alternative form of con- (“with”) (equivalent to English com- or con-) + pōtātor (“drinker”), from pōtare (“to drink”).

parole.significato: To make smaller; to press or squeeze together, or to make something occupy a smaller space or volume.
parole.testo: From Middle English compressen, from Old French compresser, from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).

parole.significato: A pricking of conscience or a feeling of regret, especially one which is slight or fleeting.
parole.testo: From Middle English compunccion, borrowed from Old French compunction, from Late Latin compunctionem (“a pricking”), from Latin compunctus, the past participle of compungere (“to severely prick”), from com- + pungere (“to prick”).

parole.significato: Agreement; accordance; consonance.
parole.testo: From Old French concordance, from Late Latin concordantia.

parole.significato: To confederate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English confederen (“to confederate; to organize a conspiracy”), borrowed from Old French confederer or directly from Late Latin confoederō. Doublet of confederate.

parole.significato: To defeat in combat; to subjugate.

parole.significato: Easily transmitted to others.
parole.testo: From Old French contagieus, from Late Latin contagiosus, from contagio.

parole.significato: Contrary or antagonistic.

parole.significato: Tending to counter, oppose, resist, argue.
parole.testo: From contrary + -ous, from Middle English contrarious, from Old French contrarious, from Late Latin contrāriōsus.

parole.significato: Able to be converted
parole.testo: From Old French convertible, from Late Latin convertibilis (“interchangeable”), from Latin convertere (“to turn back, to turn over, to turn around, to turn upside down”), from con- (“with, together”) + vertere (“to turn”), + -ibilis (“-ible: able to”). Equivalent to convert + -ible.

parole.significato: A structural member jutting out of a wall to carry a superincumbent weight.
parole.testo: From Middle English corbel, from Old French corbel, from Late Latin corbellus, corvellus, diminutive of Latin corvus (“raven”), named for the shape's resemblance to a crow's beak. Doublet of corbeau.

parole.significato: The act of corroding or the condition so produced.
parole.testo: From Middle English corrosioun, from Old French corrosion, or its source, Late Latin corrōsiōnem, accusative singular of corrōsiō (“gnawing away, corroding”), from Latin corrōdō (“gnaw away, corrode”).

parole.significato: The act of making pregnant; fertilization.

parole.significato: The act of incorporating, or the state of being incorporated.

parole.significato: Unwillingness or inability to believe; doubt about the truth or verisimilitude of something; disbelief.

parole.significato: Of an illness, condition, etc, that is unable to be cured; healless.

parole.significato: The act or process of infecting.

parole.significato: A lack or absence of gratitude; thanklessness.

parole.significato: To receive (property, a title, etc.), by legal succession or bequest, usually after the previous owner's death.

parole.significato: A pigment (or dye)-based fluid used for writing, printing etc.

parole.significato: Eager to acquire knowledge; acquisitive.

parole.significato: The property of being insensible.

parole.significato: Unable to be perceived by the senses.

parole.significato: Paying attention; attentive, heedful.

parole.significato: Communication, conversation.

parole.testo: From Middle English invisible, from Old French invisible, from Late Latin invīsibilis. Displaced native Old English unġesewenlīċ. Morphologically in- + visible. Piecewise doublet of unvisible.

parole.significato: Easily provoked to outbursts of anger; irritable.

parole.significato: Not remissible.

parole.significato: Necromancy; magic involving death.
parole.testo: From Middle English nigromauncy, from Old French nigromancie, nigremance, from Late Latin nigromantia, a blend of niger (“black”) and necromantīa (“necromancy”). Compare black art.

parole.significato: A person involved in providing direct care for the sick:
parole.testo: From Middle English norice, from Old French norrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, noun based on Latin nūtrīcius (“that which nourishes”), from nūtrīx (“wet nurse”), from nūtriō (“to suckle”).

parole.significato: The act of nourishing or nursing; tender care
parole.testo: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

parole.significato: A double curve in the shape of an elongated S; an object of that shape.

parole.significato: A large polygonal recess in a building, such as a bay window, forming a protrusion on the outer wall.
parole.testo: From Middle English oriel, from Old French oriol (“gallery, corridor”), Late Latin oriolum (“portico, hall”), probably from Latin aureolus (“gilded”), applied to an apartment decorated with gilding. See oriole. Or a diminutive of Latin os (“mouth”).

parole.significato: Relating to the origin or beginning; preceding all others.
parole.testo: From Middle English original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”), equivalent to origin + -al; see origin.

parole.significato: The furthest degree or extremity, going beyond bounds or propriety.
parole.testo: From Old French oltrance (modern outrance (“excess”)), from outrer (“pass beyond”), from oltre, outre, utre, from Late Latin ultra-. Compare outrage.

parole.significato: The art of painting.

parole.significato: To impair, to make worse.
parole.testo: From Middle English pairen, peiren, shortened form of apeiren, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, empoirier, from Late Latin peiōrō.

parole.significato: Acorns and beech mast used as forage for pigs.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French pasnage (modern French panage), from Late Latin pasnadium, pastinaticum, from pastionare (“to feed on mast, as swine”), from Latin pastio (“a pasturing, grazing”). See pastor.

parole.significato: A short narrative illustrating a lesson (usually religious/moral) by comparison or analogy.
parole.testo: From Middle English parable, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabola, parole, and palaver.

parole.significato: A package wrapped, as for shipment or transport.

parole.significato: Forgiveness for an offence.

parole.significato: An administrative part of a diocese that has its own church.

parole.significato: A conference, especially one between enemies.
parole.testo: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.

parole.significato: Existing as a part or portion; incomplete.
parole.testo: From Middle English partiall, parcial, from Old French parcial (“biased or particular”), from Late Latin partiālis (“of or pertaining to a part”), from Latin pars (“part”).

parole.significato: Able to suffer, or feel pain.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French passible, from Late Latin passibilis.

parole.significato: The part of a horse's leg between the fetlock joint and the hoof.

parole.significato: Eternal damnation.

parole.significato: Petite: small, little.

parole.significato: The opening of a vein, either to withdraw blood or for letting blood; venesection.

parole.significato: To loot or plunder by force, especially in time of war.
parole.testo: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: The highest point.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin. Doublet of panache.

parole.significato: Affectedly grand, solemn or self-important.

parole.significato: A powerful leader; a monarch; a ruler.

parole.significato: One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes…

parole.significato: The doctrine that everything has been foreordained by God or by fate.
parole.testo: From Middle English predestinacion, from Old French predestination, from Late Latin praedēstinātiō. By surface analysis, predestine + -ation. Displaced native Old English foreteohhung.

parole.significato: A definite class, state or condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).

parole.significato: Advance knowledge; foresight.
parole.testo: From Middle English previsioun, from Old French prevision, from Late Latin praevisio, praevisionem, from Latin praevideo.

parole.significato: To act as a predator.
parole.testo: From Middle English praien, prayen, preyen, partly from the noun and partly from Old French praer, preer, earlier preder, from Late Latin praedō, collateral form of Latin praedor, from praeda (“plunder, booty, loot”) + -ō (verbal suffix). Doublet of prede.

parole.significato: In the Catholic Church, a rare title conferred to or claimed by the sees of certain archbishops, or the highest-ranking…
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1275. From Middle English primat(e), from Old French primat (French primat), from Late Latin prīmās, prīmātis (“chief bishop”), substantivisation of prīmās (same as Etymology 1), from prīmus (“prime, first in rank (also as a substantive)”). parole.significato: To acquire or obtain.
parole.testo: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

parole.significato: Wasteful extravagance.
parole.testo: From prodigal + -ity, from Old French prodigalite, from Late Latin prodigalitas.

parole.significato: The act of prolonging.
parole.testo: From Middle English prolongacioun, from Old French prolongation, from Late Latin prōlongātiō, from prōlongātus, perfect passive participle of Latin prōlongō, from prō + longus. By surface analysis, prolong + -ation.

parole.significato: An advancement in rank or position.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French promocion, from Late Latin prōmotiō, from Latin prōmoveō (“to move forward”). Equivalent to promote + -ion.

parole.significato: An effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove; compare also the doublet probe.

parole.significato: One who has converted to a religion or doctrine, especially a gentile converted to Judaism.
parole.testo: From Old French proselite, from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”) (from πρός (prós, “to, towards”) and the stem -ηλυ- of ἐλήλυθα (elḗlutha), perfect of ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “come”)), translation of Hebrew גר (ger) in th

parole.significato: The process of keeping (something or someone) safe.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from stem of Late Latin prōtectiō (“a covering over”), from Latin prōtēctus, perfect passive participle of prōtegere (“to protect, cover in front”). Displaced native Old English ġesċildnes. Equivalent to protect + -ion.

parole.significato: Feeling honoured (by something); feeling happy or satisfied about an event or fact; gratified.

parole.significato: The act of provoking, inciting or annoying someone into doing something.
parole.testo: From Middle English provocacioun, from Old French provocacion, from Late Latin prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnem, from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provoke + -ation. Doublet of provokatsiya.

parole.significato: Brave, valiant, gallant.
parole.testo: From Middle English prow, from Old French prou, from Late Latin prode; more at proud.

parole.significato: domestic fowl; poultry
parole.testo: From Middle English poleyn, from Old French polain (modern French poulain), from Late Latin pullāmen; compare pullet.

parole.significato: Synonym of quadrilateral (“a polygon with four sides”).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English quadrangle, borrowed from Old French quadrangle, from Late Latin quadrangulum.

parole.significato: Often complaining; suggesting a complaint in expression; fretful, whining.
parole.testo: From Old French querelos, from Late Latin querulōsus, from Latin querulus, from queror (“to complain”).

parole.significato: The essence or inherent nature of a person or thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English quidite, from Old French quidité, and its source, Late Latin quidditās, from Latin quid (“what”) + -itas (“-ness”) (whence -ity).

parole.significato: The pear-shaped fruit of a small tree of the rose family, Cydonia oblonga.
parole.testo: From Middle English quynce, coince, a variant of coins, coin (“quince”), from Old French cooing (modern coing), from Late Latin cotōneum, from Latin mālum cotōneum, a variant of mālum Cydonium (“Cydonian apple”), translating Ancient Greek μηλοκυδώνιον (mēlokudṓnion).

parole.significato: True, genuine, not merely nominal or apparent.
parole.testo: From Middle English real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs (“matter, thing”), from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”). Doublet of realis. In modern times, likely strengthened by or conflated with the use of the prefix re-, analyzable as re- + -al.

parole.significato: To reward or repay (someone) for something done, given etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English recompensen, borrowed from Old French recompenser, from Late Latin recompensare, from Latin re- (“again”) + compensare (“to balance out”).

parole.significato: The action or process of rectifying.
parole.testo: From Middle English rectificacioun, from Old French rectificacion, from Late Latin rectificatio.

parole.significato: Royalty; sovereignty; sovereign jurisdiction.
parole.testo: From Middle English regalite, from Old French, from Late Latin rēgālitās, from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), equivalent to regal + -ity. Doublet of royalty.

parole.significato: To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.
parole.testo: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). Cognate with Old English mimorian, mymerian (“to remember, comm

parole.significato: The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection.
parole.testo: From Middle English remembraunce, from Old French remembrance, from remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorārī (“to call to mind, to remember”). Equivalent to remember + -ance.

parole.significato: To cause to become.
parole.testo: From Middle English renderen, rendren, from Old French rendre (“render, give back”), from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere (“make, give back”).

parole.significato: The act of repairing or resorting to a place.
parole.testo: From Middle English repairen (“to return”), from Old French repairier, from Late Latin repatriare (“to return to one's country”), from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repatriate.

parole.significato: A (typically scaly and egg-laying) cold-blooded vertebrate tetrapod animal, of the class Reptilia (excluding birds), su…
parole.testo: From Middle English reptil, from Old French reptile, from Late Latin rēptile, neuter of reptilis (“creeping”), from Latin rēpō (“to creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *rep- (“to creep, slink”) (Pokorny; Watkins, 1969).

parole.significato: To say something in return; to answer; to reply.
parole.testo: From Middle English respounden, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondō, from Latin respondeō. Cf. Modern French répondre.

parole.significato: A political upheaval in a government or state characterized by great change.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English revolucion, borrowed from Old French revolucion, from Late Latin revolūtiō (“the act of revolving; revolution”), from Latin revolvō (“roll back, revolve”).

parole.significato: The group of languages and cultures which are derived from Vulgar Latin.
parole.testo: From Old French romanz (“vernacular language (of France)”), from Late Latin rōmānicē, from Latin rōmānicus < rōmānus + -icus. Extended in the 17th century to all languages derived from Latin.

parole.significato: A small spiked wheel on the end of a spur of certain types.
parole.testo: From Middle English rowel, rowell, rowelle, from Old French roel, roiele (compare modern French rouelle), from Late Latin rotella, diminutive of Latin rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rotella.

parole.significato: The rescue of a ship, its crew and passengers or its cargo from a hazardous situation.
parole.testo: From Old French salver (see also save, from a variant form), from Late Latin salvare (“to make safe, secure, save”), from Latin salvus (“safe”) with the English suffix -age.

parole.significato: Possessing or conferring wisdom, especially religious wisdom.
parole.testo: From Middle English sapyencyall, from Old French or Late Latin/Ecclesiastical Latin sapientiālis, from Latin sapientia (“wisdom”) + -ālis (“-al”).

parole.significato: A bag or case with one or two shoulder straps, especially used to carry books etc.
parole.testo: First recorded circa 1340 as Middle English sachel, from Old French sachel, from Late Latin saccellum (“money bag, purse”), a diminutive of Latin sacculus, itself a diminutive of saccus (“bag”). See sack.

parole.significato: Wild; not cultivated or tamed.
parole.testo: From Middle English savage, from Old French sauvage, salvage (“wild, untamed”), from Late Latin salvāticus, alteration of Latin silvāticus (“wild”, literally “of the woods”), from silva (“forest; grove”). Doublet of sylvatic.

parole.significato: A person who saves someone, rescues another from harm.
parole.testo: First attested in 1300 as Middle English saveour, from Old French sauveour, from Late Latin salvātor, from salvō. Doublet of salvator. Displaced native Old English hǣlend.

parole.significato: Any plant in the genus Saxifraga.
parole.testo: From Old French saxifrage, from Late Latin saxifraga, from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”). Doublet of sassafras.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient West Germanic tribe that lived at the eastern North Sea coast and south of it.

parole.significato: A permanent mark on the skin, sometimes caused by the healing of a wound.

parole.significato: The act of scarifying: raking the ground harshly to remove weeds, etc.
parole.testo: From Old French scarificacion, from Late Latin scarificatio. See scarify for more.

parole.significato: The act of division, separation, cutting, cleaving, or severing; cleavage.
parole.testo: Via Middle English and Old French, from Late Latin scissio, scissionem, from Latin scindere.

parole.significato: A set of things next to each other in a set order; a series.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequence, from Old French sequence (“a sequence of cards, answering verses”), from Late Latin sequentia (“a following”), from Latin sequēns (“following”), from sequī (“to follow”); see sequent.

parole.significato: To separate from all external influence; to seclude; to withdraw.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequestren (verb) and sequestre (noun), from Old French sequestrer, from Late Latin sequestrō (“separate, give up for safekeeping”), from Latin sequester (“mediator, depositary”), probably originally meaning "follower", from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“follow”).

parole.significato: A mediaeval double-reed wind instrument with a conical wooden body.
parole.testo: From Middle English shalmuse, from Old French chalemel (modern French chalumeau), from Late Latin calamellus, from Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of caramel, chalumeau, and qalam, as well as related to calame, calamus, culm, and haulm.

parole.significato: The buying or selling of spiritual or sacred things, such as ecclesiastical offices, pardons, or consecrated objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.

parole.significato: Inauspicious, ominous, unlucky, illegitimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinistre (“unlucky”), from Old French senestre, sinistre (“left”), from Latin sinister (“left hand”).

parole.significato: Able to be dissolved.
parole.testo: From Middle English soluble, from Old French soluble, from Late Latin solūbilis, from Latin solvere (“to loosen”) + -bilis. Piecewise doublet of solvable.

parole.significato: Any of various dishes commonly made by combining liquids, such as water or stock, with other ingredients, such as meat…
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English soupe, sowpe, from Old French soupe, souppe, sope, from Late Latin suppa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô (compare Middle Dutch sope (“broth”)). Doublet of sop and zuppa. See also sup and supper. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: A spatula.
parole.testo: From Middle English spatyll, spatyl, spatule, from Old French spatule, espatule, from Late Latin spatula.

parole.significato: Explicit or definite.
parole.testo: From Old French specifique, from Late Latin specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind”) + -ific.

parole.significato: The process or act of thinking or meditating on a subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English speculacioun, speculation, from Old French speculation (compare French spéculation), from Late Latin speculātiō, speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. Morphologically speculate + -ion.

parole.significato: Characterized by speculation; based on guessing, unfounded opinions, or extrapolation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English speculatyf, borrowed from Old French speculatif or directly from Late Latin speculativus, from Latin speculor.

parole.significato: A surface in three dimensions consisting of all points equidistant from a center. .
parole.testo: From Middle English spere, from Old French sphere, from Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin. parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the spirit or the soul.
parole.testo: From Middle English spiritual, spirituel, from Old French spirituel, from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spīritus. By surface analysis, spirit + -ual.

parole.significato: A written law or ordinance passed by a legislative body.
parole.testo: From Middle English statut, from Old French statut, from Late Latin statutum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statutus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being sufficient; sufficiency.
parole.testo: From Old French sufficience, from Late Latin sufficientia.

parole.significato: The driver of a packhorse.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French sommetier (“pack-horse driver”), from Late Latin *sagmatarius, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma, “pack-saddle”).

parole.significato: Having the power to carry something or someone above, over or beyond others.
parole.testo: From Middle English superlatyf, from Old French superlatif, from Late Latin superlātīvus, from Latin superlātus (“carried above, over; extravagant, of hyperbole”), past participle of superfero (“carry over”), from super (“above”) + fero (“bear, carry”).

parole.significato: The portion of a person's name that is generally hereditary or treated as an indicator of a person's family, which may…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English surname, a partial calque of Old French surnum, surnoun (“surname; nickname”) (whence Middle English surnoun), from Late Latin supernōmen, suprānōmen (“surname”), from super- (“over, above, beyond”) and nōmen (“name”), equivalent to sur- + name.

parole.significato: Boring, monotonous, time-consuming, wearisome, livelong.
parole.testo: English tedi(um) + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

parole.significato: A species of freshwater game fish, Tinca tinca.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenche, from Old French tenche, from Late Latin tinca.

parole.significato: A male hawk or falcon.
parole.testo: From Middle English tercel, from Old French terçuel, from Late Latin tertiolus, the diminutive of Latin tertius (“third”). parole.significato: To cook lightly by browning by means of direct exposure to a fire or other heat source.
parole.testo: From Middle English tosten, from Old French toster (“to roast, grill”), from Late Latin tostō, -āre, frequentative of torreō (“to burn, grill”) from its perfect passive participle tostus (“grilled, burnt”).

parole.significato: Whatever impedes activity, progress, or freedom, such as a net or shackle.
parole.testo: From Middle English trameyle, from Old French tramail (“net for catching fish”), from Late Latin tremaculum, from tri- (“tri-”) + macula (“spot, speck; mesh, cell”). Cognate with Italian tramaglio (“trammel”), Spanish trasmallo (“drift net”).

parole.significato: A violation of a law, duty or commandment.
parole.testo: From Middle English transgressioun, from Old French transgression, from Late Latin trānsgressiō, from Latin trānsgressus (perfect active participle of trānsgredior (“to step across”)) + -iō.

parole.significato: Change, alteration.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, from Old French transmutacion (“transformation, metamorphosis”), from Late Latin transmutationem, from Latin transmutare (“to change”).

parole.significato: To uproot (a growing plant), and plant it in another place.
parole.testo: From Middle English transplaunten, from Old French transplanter, from Late Latin transplantare, equivalent to trans- + plant.

parole.significato: To shake, quiver, or vibrate.
parole.testo: From Middle English tremblen, from Old French trembler, from Late Latin tremulāre, ultimately from Latin tremere (“quiver, shake”). Cognate with Ancient Greek τρέμω (trémō).

parole.testo: From Middle English tribulation, from Old French tribulacion, from Late Latin trībulātiō (“distress, trouble, tribulation, affliction”), from Latin tribulāre (“to press, probably also thresh out grain”), from trībulum (“a sledge consisting of a wooden block studded with sharp pieces of flint or with

parole.significato: Any of several species of fish in Salmonidae, closely related to salmon, and distinguished by spawning more than once.

parole.significato: A short staff, a club; a cudgel.
parole.testo: From Middle English tronchoun, from Old French tronchon (“thick stick”), from Late Latin *troncionem, from Latin truncus.

parole.significato: A bunch of feathers, grass or hair, etc., held together at the base.
parole.testo: From Middle English tuft, toft, tofte, an alteration of earlier *tuffe (> Modern English tuff), from Old French touffe, tuffe, toffe, tofe (“tuft”) (modern French touffe), from Late Latin tūfa (“helmet crest”) (near Vegezio). parole.significato: The act of uniting or joining two or more things into one.
parole.testo: From Middle English unyoun, from Old French union, from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”). Doublet of unio.

parole.significato: Not limited or restricted; unrestrained; limitless.
parole.testo: From trammel (“fishing net; shackle”), from Old French tramail (“net for catching fishes”), from Late Latin tremaculum.

parole.significato: A person on a trip of indeterminate destination and/or length of time.
parole.testo: From Old French vagabond, from Late Latin vagābundus, from Latin vagari (“wander”). Compare moribund.

parole.significato: Able to be forgiven; worthy of forgiveness.
parole.testo: From Old French venial, borrowed from Late Latin veniālem (“pardonable”), from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to words.
parole.testo: From Old French verbal, from Late Latin verbālis (“belonging to a word”). Equivalent to verb + -al.

parole.significato: A green colour, now only in heraldry; represented in engraving by diagonal parallel lines 45 degrees counter-clockwise.
parole.testo: From Middle English vert, borrowed from Old French vert, from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Doublet of virid, which was borrowed directly from Latin.

parole.significato: A craft for transportation on or in water, air, or space.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vessel, vessell (“small container”); from Old French vaissel (compare modern French vaisseau and Catalan vaixell), from Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vase, vessel”).

parole.significato: To debase; to degrade .
parole.testo: Probably from Middle English vilein, from Old French vilein (modern French vilain), in turn from Late Latin vīllānus, meaning serf or peasant, someone who is bound to the soil of a Latin vīlla, which is to say, worked on the equivalent of a plantation in late Antiquity, in Italy or Gaul. parole.significato: Able to be seen.
parole.testo: From Middle English visible, from Old French visible, from Late Latin visibilis (“that may be seen”), from Latin videre (“to see”), past participle visus; see vision. Displaced native Old English ġesewenlīċ.

parole.significato: To bring to life; to enliven.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French vivifier, from Late Latin vivificō.

parole.significato: A kind of fine white bread or cake.
parole.testo: From Middle English wastel, from Old French wastel, gastel (> French gâteau), from Late Latin wastellum, from Frankish *wastil, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *wistiz (“sustenance, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to be”).
